sentences.text: Ornithopsis is a dubious extinct genus of titanosauriform sauropod dinosaur containing only one known species, Ornithopsis hulkei.
The only currently valid species is O. hulkei, which is known only from fragmentary remains.
The holotype of Ornithopsis hulkei consists of a single vertebra centrum that lacks a neural spine.
The holotype vertebra is heavily pneumatized, containing large internal cavities known as camellae.
The holotype vertebra is narrow and tall, features a ridge on its underside, is opisthocoelous, and possesses a deep subtriangular pleurocoel located posteriorly over two-thirds of its length.
The genus name Ornithopsis means "bird-like face" and reflects Seeley's belief that the animal was an intermediate form between pterosaurs, birds, and dinosaurs.
Seeley identified the fossils as vertebrae with internal cavities for air sacs, a feature seen in pterosaurs and modern birds.
Ornithopsis hulkei was a large sauropod that reached a length of 24 meters.
The type species Ornithopsis hulkei was named and described by Harry Govier Seeley in 1870.
The type material consisted of two dorsal vertebrae found in East Sussex and on the Isle of Wight.
In 1882, Richard Lydekker Hulke described the pelvis material NHMUK PV R 97 from the Wealden deposits as a new species named Ornithopsis eucamerotus.

In 1887, Hulke described additional material including vertebrae, ribs, and a pelvis collected by Alfred Nicholson Leeds from the Eyesbury Jurassic deposits of Northamptonshire as the new species Ornithopsis leedsii.
The specimens identified as Ornithopsis leedsii were collected in May 1892 and are stored under catalog numbers NHMUK PV R 1985-1988.
In 1874, Hulke named the humerus specimen Ischyrosaurus, suggesting a close relationship to Cetiosaurus oxoniensis and other related genera.
The animal possessed a typical brachiosaurid nasal arch, had front legs longer than its hind legs, was herbivorous, and moved on four legs.
Comparisons with Giraffatitan estimate the holotype specimen of Ornithopsis hulkei to be between 16 and 18 meters in length.
Ornithopsis leedsii was distinguished from other Ornithopsis specimens by its much larger size, robusticity, and older age, despite similarities in vertebrae and pelvis structure.
The genus Ornithopsis was established by Seeley in 1870.
Ornithopsis hulkei is classified within the unranked family Titanosauriformes.
Ornithopsis belongs to the parent group Titanosauriformes.
Ornithopsis eucamerotus is a nomen dubium synonymized with Chondrosteosaurus gigas.
Ornithopsis leedsii is a nomen dubium that is indeterminate beyond Eusauropoda.
Cetiosaurus leedsi was later assigned to an intermediate member of Brachiosauridae, with debate over whether it was a proper species of Ornithopsis or an indeterminate eusauropod.

In an early 1927 review, Friedrich von Huene retained Ornithopsis greppini in the genus, considering it part of a group containing O. hulkei, O. leedsii, O. humerocristatus, O. manseli, and O. (?) greppini.
The fossil range of Ornithopsis hulkei is the Early Cretaceous period.
Ornithopsis lived in the early Cretaceous, approximately 130 million years ago during the Barremian stage, in what is now Europe.
The genus Ornithopsis has a recorded time range from the Tithonian to the Aptian (145.06 to 119.57 million years ago).
Ornithopsis is a genus of sauropod dinosaur known from the Early Cretaceous of England and possibly Germany.
A fragmentary dorsal vertebra attributed to Ornithopsis was found in northwestern Germany and dates to the Late Barremian-Early Aptian.
John Hulke synonymized the genera Eucamerotus and Chondrosteosaurus with Ornithopsis based on shared unique internal vertebral structures.
The type vertebra of Ornithopsis possesses unique lateral compression and a ventral ridge, identifying it as a diagnostic titanosauriform.
The referral of the German specimen to Ornithopsis is considered tentative due to poor preservation.
A 2010 overview noted that Ornithopsis manseli shares features with both Rebbachisauridae and Titanosauriformes but lacks sufficient characteristics to determine its exact phylogenetic position.
Richard Owen rejected Seeley's creation of the genus Ornithopsis and his evolutionary interpretation of the material.
